digo: matsere (northern Digo) / pemba, mapemba (southern Digo); cob tsere
digo_source: Mgombato ('matsere corn, maize'; 'pemba maize'; 'tsere maize cob'); Pakia (Matsere N, Mapemba S)

teaser.en: North of the Digo country maize is *matsere*; in the south it is *pemba*, and both are ground into flour for *ugali*.

summary.en: *Matsere* is maize, the main rain-fed cereal of Digo farms. It is ground into flour for *ugali*, roasted on the cob and baked with bananas into *mabumbunda*.

about.en:
*Matsere* is a tall cereal grass with broad, strap-shaped leaves and a tassel of male flowers at the top of the stem. The cobs (*tsere*) form lower down, wrapped in husks, each sending out a tuft of silk.

Digo farmers grow both local cultivars and modern hybrids. The local kinds are named by grain colour: *maricheni* (yellow), *chitweka* (black), *mwatsaka* (red), *tsere ra matungo* (mixed) and *mjundo* (striped). Hybrids such as *kosti* and *katumani* are also grown.

where.en: Maize is the main rain-fed cereal of Kwale farms, planted with the rains and often intercropped with cassava and cowpeas. After harvest the grain is stored in the granary, the *chitsaga*.

uses.en:
The dried grain is ground into flour (*sima* or *dona*) for *ugali*, the stiff porridge eaten across East Africa. Fresh cobs are roasted over coals. Maize flour and bananas are combined to make *mabumbunda*, a maize-banana bread.

After harvest the stalks, *buwa*, are left in the field.

culture.en: Maize farming carries a whole body of Digo know-how, from choosing seed to storing the grain in the *chitsaga*. The red cultivar *mwatsaka* shares its name with the Digo word for chilli pepper.

names.en: Digo: *matsere* in northern Digo and *pemba* or *mapemba* in southern Digo; the cob is *tsere*. Swahili: *mahindi*. English: maize or corn. Scientists call it *Zea mays*.

reason.en: Sorghum, another cereal ground for porridge
Cassava, grown in the same fields
Banana, mixed with maize in mabumbunda
Chilli, which shares a name with red maize

definition.en: The maize cob; Pakia notes the word is used for the maize plant as well. Matsere (the plural) is the usual word for maize.

meaning.en: From an old Bantu word for 'cleaned grain'; the change to tsere keeps it apart from mtele, cleaned rice.

definition.en: The male flower at the top of the maize plant. Farmers watch it as a sign of ripeness: when it dries, the cob is ready to harvest. One respondent also called it thamra, a word other Digo did not know.

meaning.en: Probably from mphunga, rice, which has a similar flower head.

shared_with: punga: the florets of the coconut flower
punga: the flowering panicles of grasses and sugarcane

definition.en: The young female flower of maize, the cob in its early growth wrapped in its husk. Unlike the tassel, it counts as a ruwa (flower) because it bears fruit.

meaning.en: Sheath: the husk covers the growing cob as a sheath covers a knife.

definition.en: The female flower of maize, the part that becomes the cob (labelled in Pakia's Fig. 3.4).
The female flower of maize, known only from the growth-stage phrase ganatuluza-ndamba, 'producing female flowers'.
The silks, the long threads hanging from the tip of the cob. They appear in the sixth month (described as ganasonga, 'plaiting'); when they are lost (matsere ganakata njio) the cob is mature.

meaning.en: Also the name of a colourful hanging costume worn by traditional dancers.

definition.en: The milky juice in maize grains at the milk stage; its presence shows the grain is not yet mature.
The hard core of the maize cob. Mgombato spells it guguta (class ma): a cob with the grains removed.
The stalk left standing after the maize has been harvested.

mgombato: tsere (ma) maize cob; mahindi. (See: matsere, pembe)
